title: Lobbying firms paid with public money
question: Which firms that lobby City officials for private clients are also paid by the City, or by nonprofits the City funds?
finding: 4 firms that sell lobbying appear by name in the City’s payment ledger, paid $1.4 million since fiscal 2019, the largest Hanson Bridgett LLP ($662,737). 7 firm-and-nonprofit pairs appear on City-funded nonprofits’ tax returns among the highest-paid contractors ($4.6 million), and lobbyists’ own reports show $2.9 million in lobbying fees from nonprofits the City funds. Of 10 names that file as lobbyists on the City’s behalf to other governments, 0 also appear as a firm lobbying City officials.
how: Firms that sell lobbying (three or more outside clients) are matched by name to: the Controller’s payment ledger for fiscal 2019 to 2026; the five-highest-paid-contractors table on the tax returns of City-funded nonprofits (latest version of each return); their own reported fees from clients that are City-funded nonprofits; and the Ethics Commission’s reports from lobbyists acting for the City before other governments. What the City pays its State and federal lobbyists is in the site’s “State politics and State grants” page and the site’s “Federal politics and relief money” page.
limits: A City payment to a firm with a lobbying arm is usually for something else: legal work, communications, planning or engineering. A law firm on a nonprofit’s return was most likely paid for legal services. Tax returns list only contractors paid more than $100,000 and only the top five, so smaller engagements are invisible. Name matches can join different firms. Lobbying is registered, and so is giving by a lobbyist’s clients and colleagues.
